> It's worse because you regen a little bit of your missing mana throughout the entire 5 seconds with Mana Font, whereas with Meditation you've already regened 5 seconds worth of mana (based on your base MP5) before gaining that burst of 1.5% missing mana.

This doesn't make sense. I can present an alternate way of looking at it. Say you have 0 mana at t=0s. At t=0s, you get a burst of 1.5% missing mana. Then for the next 5 seconds, you regenerate mana normally. Viewed this way, the burst regen is actually more efficient than the chalice style, because you get 5 seconds worth of regen immediately, and before the amount regenerated is lessened by your natural regen. 

So is the burst regen better or worse than the trickle regen? It depends on the timing of the ticks and when you expend your mana. Let's say you have a pool of 500 mana and somehow your full combo costs 300 mana. Every 5 seconds, meditation ticks. If you cast your combo right after a tick, then you get your scenario and burst regen is worse than trickle regen. If you cast your combo right before a tick, then you get my scenario and burst regen is better than trickle regen. In practice, you wouldn't actually time your spells based on a fairly opaque mastery like this (you could, and you'd get slightly better mana efficiency, but it's probably better just to optimize your spell timing for actually important stuff like hitting the opponent or farming). So you're going to get the good case and the bad case roughly 50% of the time each. Therefore there is no expected difference in efficiency between the meditation style of regen and the chalice style. (I think meditation should still be changed to use the chalice style however, just because it's simpler). 

tl;dr: you're wrong. about half the time, the opposite scenario occurs which makes up for what you described. the actual result is that there is no difference in efficiency.

With lifesteal: If you are stronger, you are guaranteed to win lane (because you can trade and heal, while they get zoned). You can afford to make mistakes because you can heal back up quickly.

Without lifesteal: you are stronger, but your victory isn't assured. You can still get poked out of lane, or at least to the point where the enemy can fight you. If you pick a fight, you'll be able to win, but if you play carelessly (getting hit by random attacks or support poke), you don't have a crutch to fall back on.

If your entire team has x hp, then rainbow latents on one monster gives you x*(1/0.99-1) effective HP. HP latents give y*1.075 effective HP, where y is the HP of the monster. Therefore, HP latents are better when y*1.075 > x*(1/0.99-1), or y/x > 0.0094 (i.e. the monster must contribute more than 0.94% of the team's HP, which is almost always true). This is for the case of only one latented monster on a team. Resists become more powerful the more of them you stack, and HP latents don't apply to plusses (5940 extra HP in total) so we'll consider the fully pentamaxed case as well. A team of all rainbow latents has (x+5940)/0.95 effective HP, whereas a HP latented team has x*1.075+5940 effective HP. HP latents are better when x*1.075+5940 > (x+5940)/0.95, or x*1.075+5940 > x*1.052 + 6252.63, i.e. when x > 13976.47 HP, which again is easily achievable by almost any team. 

In conclusion, if you want to increase the raw tankiness of your team in general, HP latents will always give you more effective HP than rainbow latents. Color resists are more effective if you're stacking them to counter a specific threat (like DQ Hera), but spreading them out in a rainbow fashion is ineffective except as a counter to 100% gravities. It's also worth noting that rainbow latents will also make recovery more effective, but in general colour > HP > rainbow for meeting thresholds.

Okay, I was just letting you know that the main weakness of the match-5 playstyle is that it can't really use the good damage awakenings (TPA and rows). So a match-5 leader is going to be outdamaged by a TPA or row leader with a lower LS atk multiplier in many cases.

Killer awakenings will improve your damage, but they are rare, situational, and detrimental in some cases. 

Stacking huge numbers of oe awakenings (e.g. a deity or a specific character) will improve your damage somewhat, but your team already has a huge number of those. 

The easiest way to deal more damage is to stop running a rainbow team and focus on one color. Monocolor always deals more than multicolor, all else being held equal. It's simply because you can't get the full benefit of orb changers if you don't stay monocolor. If you pop a specific character, your green subs don't deal any damage. If you create fire orbs with an active skill, only he benefits from those. You should change your specific character over to the red form as soon as possible. 

Also, you need to make more combos. You can make it easier by using the time extend badge and adding more time extend subs, but you should also watch some tutorials on how to combo efficiently. 

**Main takeaway: focus on one color and making more combos.**

> Doesn't going mono color make damage kind of inconsistent though?

> Right now I don't really have to rely on my actives much at all for matching, as there is almost always something I can do. I would also get screwed if something resists/absorbs red if that's all I have. I guess that's where you rely on your sub color?

I understand exactly the reason you want to have a rainbow-ish team (it's a mistake a lot of new players make), but it really hurts your damage a lot. Not making enough combos is the root of all your problems. Let's say you erase 5 red orbs to deal damage. If you make no other combos, you obviously won't have any more red orbs next turn. If you matched the entire board (30 orbs), you will get 30 fresh orbs and 1/6 of them will be red. Thus you'll have another 5 red orbs ready to go next turn and you won't need actives on average. Matching all 30 orbs is a bit unrealistic, but a good player should be able to match at least 6-7 combos on any board. That translates to ~20 orbs cleared or ~3 fire orbs dropping each turn. Typically you pop orb change actives to create fire orbs when you run out, but with good comboing and smart orb conservation you don't need to do this too often.

> I'm also using the time extend badge already, but it's not much time for matching.

Watch [this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tLku-s20EBE) and practice. Aim to make 6 combos each turn. That should be doable with the time extend badge and a couple of time extends on your team.

Edit: With a match-5 w/ enhance leader, it's even more important that you run a mono color team. The bonus ATK applies only for the element that you matched 5 for, which means that most of your team doesn't even get the full multiplier.

With 2 row awakenings, matching rows isn't even better than matching separate size-3 combos, without even factoring other awakenings. A normal row team has at least 10 rows, and some teams might even have up to 20 rows.

It's just better to focus on as few colors as possible in this game. Even combo teams and rainbow teams try to keep the entire team the same color. 

That being said, I think the closest thing to what you're looking for are rainbow leaders (Ra Dragon, Reincarnated Ra, Sherias Roots for some examples). These leaders activate by matching all colors (or almost all colors). Because these teams cannot use orb changers without removing colors they need to activate, they cannot heavily stack one color and thus would deal significantly less damage than comparable row leaders. Therefore, these leaders typically have massive ATK multipliers to make up for this fact (e.g. 225x for Ra). Even so, 225x rainbow still only deals roughly the same damage as the burst of a 64x row leader. 

Rainbow teams need to have one of each color on the team, either as a main attribute or a subattribute. People still tend to favor keeping the main attributes "on-color" (because that simplifies matching TPAs), but sometimes the best utility actives are in a different color and so rainbow teams are the most likely to have off-color subs.

To play a rainbow team, needless to say you need to combo well. Most of the frustrations of playing a rainbow team will come from boards that are not activatable, i.e. boards without the all colors you need. That's why it's essential to have roughly 2 Kali style board changers on your team so you can fix a bad board.

When stamina is implemented correctly (i.e. not too restrictive, and not tacked on), it actually prevents players from getting burnt out and improves the players' enjoyment of the game. You can't just tack stamina onto any generic game and expect it to work; you need to build the game around the stamina system to have it be satisfying to the player. 

A certain popular mobile puzzle game is a very good example of a successful stamina system that lets players play a reasonable amount and creates a metagame of planning out stamina use, in addition to being monetization for the game. Stamina regenerates at 1 per 3 minutes, players generally have 200-300 max stamina, and $1 is a full stamina refill (although this is something that most players rarely purchase). Ranking up will also fully restore stamina, and so  there is a lot of planning that goes into maximizing stamina use by ranking up at strategic times. Most dungeons cost 25 or 50 stamina to run. Some dungeons are challenging and take upwards of half an hour to play, while others are trivial to beat in less than a minute. So the player has flexibility in whether they want the stamina to last by playing hard, rewarding dungeons or whether they just want to burn it quickly to get lesser rewards. 

In fact, there are occasionally scenarios where you can earn enough XP from a dungeon that you can use rank ups to refill stamina and run it infinitely. While that seems nice on paper, it actually feels like a bit of a chore. It's nice when you do run out of stamina and then you can stop playing without feeling like you're wasting resources.
